craft:Do this one.name: Kameni otok, Postira (Brač)
craft:Do this one.teaser: Two hours with a point, a claw chisel and a block of the white Brač limestone the palace is made of
craft:Do this one.story: Brač has been cutting its white limestone since the Romans quarried it for Diocletian, and the craft never stopped: the stonemasons' school at Pučišća has taught hand carving since 1909 and still sends students to win prizes at the Verona stone fair. On the north coast at Postira, a small outfit called Kameni otok, stone island, sits a few visitors at a bench with the real tools: point, claw chisel, hammer. A certified master stonemason guides your hand while the dust settles white on your sleeves, and you leave with the piece you cut. Missing: the master is not named in any listing we found.
craft:Do this one.why: The only hands-on craft near Split you can book like a table, and it uses the stone you have been walking on all week.
facts: Carve your own small piece of Brač stone with traditional tools under a certified stonemason; tools, stone and the finished piece included
About two hours, plus the Split to Supetar ferry and a short drive east to Postira
Listed at about AU$131 a head on a resale site (Oct 2026); ask the workshop for its euro price

Ahead, through the operator or the listing; meeting point signed Kameni otok on the road out of Postira. Check the season: island activities thin out from November. For the school itself, Pučišća opens its workshops to visitors mainly on summer mornings

craft:Other one.name: Filigran Split, Bosanska 4
craft:Other one.teaser: A family of silver filigree makers a few steps from the Pjaca, twisting wire the slow way
craft:Other one.story: In a narrow shop on Bosanska, just outside the palace walls, the Čivljak family sells silver filigree they make themselves: Dalmatian buttons, drop earrings, the round jerma beads of old costume, twisted and soldered from wire as fine as thread. Viktor Čivljak learned it from his father, and in 2014 he was described as the only jeweller in Split still working entirely by hand; his son Lorenc was training as the fourth generation. One pair of earrings takes eight or nine hours, which is why most jewellers moved to casting. Croatia has no trade school for filigree; you learn it at a family bench. Missing: a class. You can watch and buy, not learn.
craft:Other one.why: Buy filigree from the hands that soldered it, five minutes from the Peristyle.
facts: Look at the pieces, ask how the wire is worked, buy direct or commission a traditional piece
Priced by silver weight and hours; no current prices checked
No class and no booking. The business is listed active at Bosanska 4 (company register, Oct 2026), but we found no 2026 opening hours: walk by in shop hours

sources.label: Tricia Anne Mitchell, Croatian filigree jewelry, Bosanska 4 (2014)

craft:Other two.name: The Benedictine nuns of Hvar
craft:Other two.teaser: Lace made from the thread inside agave leaves, by a convent of nuns in Hvar town
craft:Other two.story: Behind a plain wall in Hvar town, in the house that once belonged to the Renaissance poet Hanibal Lucić, Benedictine nuns have lived since 1664. They make lace from fibres drawn out of the long grey-green leaves of the agave that grows on the island: the leaf is soaked, the pale threads pulled free, then worked into small, stiff, ivory medallions that take weeks each. Lacemaking in Croatia, Hvar's agave lace among it, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list. The convent museum shows the lace with the nuns' paintings and church silver, and pieces are for sale, at prices that reflect the hours. Missing: a lesson. The nuns make it; visitors only look and buy.
craft:Other two.why: Agave lace exists nowhere else; this is the only place to see it made into something.
facts: Visit the convent museum, see the lace, buy a piece
Half an hour inside, on a day on Hvar
No current entry fee or lace prices checked
No booking and no class. Hours not confirmed for late October: check with the convent or the Hvar tourist office before the crossing, and mind the winter catamaran timetable

craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.name: What is sold as Dalmatian craft
craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.teaser: Cheap 'Hvar lace' and shiny 'filigree' in the palace alleys rarely came off a Dalmatian bench
craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.story: Walk the stalls between the Peristyle and the Riva and the same three crafts repeat: lace, silver filigree and white stone. Each is slow by nature. Real Hvar agave lace is made by one convent of nuns, a medallion over weeks, so a pile of cheap 'Hvar lace' on a stall cannot be theirs. A pair of hand-made filigree earrings costs a Split craftsman eight or nine hours, which is why most jewellery sold as filigree is now cast in a mould. Brač stone is cut by hand at a few workshops on the island; a stall cannot tell you who carved its piece. If a seller cannot name the maker and the place, assume nobody here made it.
craft:What is sold as Dalmatian craft.why: Ask who made it and where; the real makers in this section answer with a name.
facts: Turn the piece over: hand filigree shows tiny solder joints and slightly uneven loops, cast work is smooth and identical; agave lace is stiff and ivory, not soft white cotton. Ask the seller for the maker's name
Filigran Split on Bosanska for filigree, the Benedictine convent in Hvar town for agave lace, Kameni otok or the Pučišća school on Brač for stone (each has its own card in this section)

linger:D16 Coffee.name: D16 Coffee
linger:D16 Coffee.teaser: Split's own specialty roaster, in a dim palace alley with a few tables on the stone outside
linger:D16 Coffee.story: D16 roasts its own beans and pours them in a small, low room on Dominisova, a lane inside the palace's western half, with a handful of tables in the alley outside. This is the cup locals point to when you ask for coffee rather than a terrace: a V60 of a rotating Ethiopian single origin, a proper espresso, a cold brew in the heat. The room is dark and the music can run loud, so for real work use the second, larger D16 at Trogirska 8, just outside the walls. Old notes that placed it at Dosud 9 were wrong.
linger:D16 Coffee.why: The best filter coffee in Split, before the palace fills.
facts: Dominisova 16, inside the palace; second bar at Trogirska 8
Listed 07:00–19:00 (In Your Pocket, May 2026); other listings differ, check in winter
A V60 of the Ethiopian single origin, or a cold brew
An hour at Dominisova; longer at Trogirska 8, the roomier one. Wi-Fi and plugs not confirmed

linger:The Riva.name: The Riva
linger:The Riva.teaser: Split's waterfront living room: white paving, palms, and the palace's south wall at your back
linger:The Riva.story: The Riva runs along the south face of the palace, the wall where Diocletian's rooms once looked straight onto the water. Its present form is the Zagreb studio 3LHD's: a competition won in 2005, opened on 7 May 2007, Sudamja day, with pale concrete slabs, low green islands of Mediterranean planting and white awnings over the café tables. Sit with a coffee or a glass of Pošip and the whole port moves past: ferries for Brač and Hvar, island catamarans, fishermen heading for Matejuška. Step through to the Prokurative behind, the long arcaded square begun in 1859 to Vicko Andrić's design.
linger:The Riva.why: An hour at a Riva table is how Split watches itself; go before the works start.
facts: The waterfront below the palace's south wall, from the Prokurative (Trg Republike) east to the ferry port
Always; café terraces from morning to late
A Pošip by the glass or a kava s mlijekom; prices vary terrace to terrace, none checked

No: for watching, not typing. Note: drinking alcohol you carry yourself on the Riva is fined under the city's Public Order Act. The city plans a new 3LHD makeover, with works expected to begin around November 2026 in phases (Croatia Week, Oct 2026): expect fenced sections

linger:Matejuška with a bottle.name: Matejuška with a bottle
linger:Matejuška with a bottle.teaser: No bar, no waiter: the fishermen's harbour at dusk, a bottle, and half of Split on the quay
linger:Matejuška with a bottle.story: At the western end of the Riva the paving gives way to the small fishermen's harbour of Matejuška, where wooden gajete and pasaras lie nose to the quay and nets dry on the stone. Toward evening people drift down with a bottle from a shop, some pršut in paper and a few tomatoes, and sit on the blocks with their legs over the water while the light goes behind Marjan. Nobody serves you and nobody moves you on. Out of season it is a neighbourhood thing; in summer the crowd is younger and thicker. Fife, across the road, is the place if you want a plate.
linger:Matejuška with a bottle.why: The one stretch of Split waterfront where you sit with locals, not with a menu.
facts: Matejuška, the fishermen's harbour at the west end of the Riva, below Veli Varoš
Nothing: bring a bottle from a shop and a glass
No. Split fines drinking in public in the old town and on the Riva (EUR 300 under the Public Order Act); a local guide names Matejuška as the legal alternative, but check the signs on the day

drink:Plavac Mali.name: Plavac Mali
drink:Plavac Mali.teaser: Little blue: the dark, warm red of every Dalmatian table, grown on slopes that face the sea
drink:Plavac Mali.story: Plavac Mali means little blue, for the small dark berries. It is the red you will be poured from Split to the islands, and at its best it comes from the south face of the Pelješac peninsula, where Dingač and Postup drop toward the water and the vines take sun from the sky, the sea and the white stones. DNA work showed it to be the child of Tribidrag, the grape the world knows as Zinfandel, and Dobričić from the island of Šolta, a few miles off Split. How that was found out is told in the history fold. In the glass it is ripe, dried-cherry fruit, grippy tannin and alcohol that often passes 14%.
drink:Plavac Mali.why: Drink it with peka lamb or brodet, when its weight and tannin have something to hold on to.
facts: Deep ruby, dried cherry and fig, firm tannin, 14% and up
Plavac Mali; the protected slopes appear as Dingač or Postup
A Dingač or Postup; the old guide named Saints Hills and Korta Katarina (seen May 2026). Paradox and Zinfandel pour it by the glass

sources.label: Wine Spectator, Researchers solve mystery of Zinfandel's origins

drink:Pošip.name: Pošip
drink:Pošip.teaser: Korčula's white, protected in 1967 before any other Croatian white wine
drink:Pošip.story: Pošip grows almost only on Korčula, in the linked fields of Čara and Smokvica at the island's centre. Island tradition says Marin Tomašić of Smokvica found the vine in the nineteenth century; the sources disagree on the year. In 1967 it became the first Croatian white wine given legal protection of origin. DNA shows it to be a cross of two other Korčula grapes, Bratkovina and Zlatarica blatska. It makes a broad white with soft acidity, citrus peel, apricot, almond and a salty last note, fresh from steel or rounder from the barrel.
drink:Pošip.why: The white with weight enough for grilled fish, crni rižot or a plate of Pag cheese.
facts: Straw gold, citrus peel, apricot, almond, a saline finish; soft acidity
Pošip, often with Čara or Smokvica
Toreta, Bire, Krajančić or the Pošip Čara cooperative (producers named in the old guide, seen May 2026)

drink:Tribidrag.name: Tribidrag
drink:Tribidrag.teaser: The grape California calls Zinfandel, made again by a dozen families in Kaštela, just west of Split
drink:Tribidrag.story: The grape that became Zinfandel in California and Primitivo in Puglia is back in bottle where it was found, in the Kaštela villages strung along the bay between Split and Trogir. Twelve local growers now carry the Kaštelanski crljenak origin label, among them Anton Kovač of Putalj, whose vines climb the slopes of Kozjak above Kaštel Sućurac and who shows visitors the barrel room, the Matela family next door, and Kaštel Sikuli in Kaštel Novi. Expect a lighter, juicier red than a California Zin: red cherry, pepper, a dry finish. The story of how it was found is told in the history fold.
drink:Tribidrag.why: Drink Zinfandel's ancestor fifteen minutes from where it was found, poured by the people who replanted it.
facts: Mid-ruby, red cherry and plum, pepper, fresher and less jammy than a California Zinfandel
Crljenak kaštelanski or Kaštelanski crljenak, Tribidrag; sometimes Zinfandel for export

Putalj (Anton Kovač) or Matela from Kaštel Sućurac, or Kaštel Sikuli, whose 2022 Kaštelanski crljenak scored 92 in Falstaff (2026). Putalj takes visitors by booking; Zinfandel Food & Wine Bar pours Tribidrag in town

drink:Vugava.name: Vugava
drink:Vugava.teaser: Vis's own white, called Bugava on the island, poured in a cellar cut into an old army tunnel
drink:Vugava.story: Vugava is a white grape almost nobody grows outside Vis, the farthest of the inhabited islands off Split, where they call it Bugava. It makes a full, golden, softly aromatic white, apricot and honey with a line of salt, that can take a few years in bottle. Antonio Lipanović is the name you will find most easily: the largest grower, he ages his wine in a tunnel the Yugoslav army cut into the island, and pours Vugava, Plavac Mali and Prošek there. On Vis, Roki's, Senjanović and Ivčević also make it; on Brač, Stina is the rare exception.
drink:Vugava.why: Bring a bottle home: outside Vis you will rarely see it on a list.
facts: Golden, apricot, honey, Mediterranean herbs, saline; full and soft
Vugava, or Bugava, often with Vis or Viška
Lipanović, Roki's, Senjanović or Ivčević from Vis; Stina from Brač

sources.label: Total Croatia News, The indigenous grapes of Croatia: Vugava
Total Croatia News, Antonio Lipanović

drink:Prošek.name: Prošek
drink:Prošek.teaser: A sweet wine of sun-dried grapes, not a sparkling, whatever the name sounds like
drink:Prošek.story: Prošek is made by laying grapes out on racks until they shrivel, then pressing the concentrated juice into a sweet, amber or garnet wine of around 14%: Plavac Mali for the red, Maraština or Bogdanuša for the white. Dalmatian cooks pour it into the pašticada pot, and families open it for guests with dry figs or almonds. It has nothing to do with Prosecco, the Italian sparkling wine, but the names collide. The EU refused to protect Prošek in 2013; in 2021 the Commission took Croatia's new application as admissible and published it, and Italy objected. We found no final ruling.
drink:Prošek.why: A small glass at the end of dinner, with rožata or a few dried figs.
facts: Amber or garnet, raisin, dried fig, honey; sweet, around 14%
Prošek, often with the grape; Croatian producers have also used Dalmatian sweet wine terms while the name is contested
A Prošek from a named grower; ask for 'sweet dessert wine', not 'Prosecco'. Lipanović on Vis makes one

drink:Rakija.name: Rakija
drink:Rakija.teaser: Plum, pear, walnut or a fistful of island herbs, at 40% and at any hour
drink:Rakija.story: Rakija is the clear fruit spirit of the whole region, and every house seems to have a bottle. Šljivovica is plum; kruškovac pear; orahovac is dark and bitter-sweet from green walnuts; medica is softened with honey. The Dalmatian one is travarica: grape spirit steeped with sage, rosemary, fennel and whatever grows on the hill, sometimes with the sprigs left in the bottle. A farmer's bottle from the market often beats the supermarket one. Zadar's Maraska, a postwar company heir to the city's old maraschino trade, is the familiar industrial label.
drink:Rakija.why: Accept the glass when it is offered; it is how a Dalmatian host says welcome.
facts: Clear or golden, around 40%; travarica smells of sage and rosemary

sources.label: Wikipedia, Maraska (founding date)

bars:Paradox.name: Paradox
bars:Paradox.teaser: Taste Dalmatia against the continent: Dingač beside a Plešivica sparkler, cheese on the board
bars:Paradox.story: Use Paradox to taste across the map in one sitting: a Dingač or Postup from Pelješac, a Pošip from Korčula, then something from the cool north, a Plešivica sparkling wine or a continental white, with Pag cheese between glasses. Ask the person pouring to line up three Plavac Mali from different slopes and the difference in sun shows at once. It is the after-dinner stop more than the aperitif.
bars:Paradox.why: The one place to compare Croatia's coast and continent glass by glass.
facts: A Plavac Mali from Dingač, a Korčula Pošip and a Pag cheese board
After dinner; it keeps late hours
Walk in. Check it is trading first: an undated listing marks it closed and we found no 2026 confirmation

sources.label: Time Out Croatia, Wine & Cheese Bar Paradox

bars:Zinfandel.name: Zinfandel
bars:Zinfandel.teaser: Where to taste Kaštela's Tribidrag in the old town, next to a Babić from the north
bars:Zinfandel.story: The bar is named after the grape, so start there: a glass of Tribidrag from Kaštela, then a Plavac Mali to taste the child against its parent. The list runs the length of Croatia, about fifteen wines by the glass in MICHELIN's count, so add a Babić from the Šibenik hills for a drier, leaner Dalmatian red. Small plates keep it from becoming a long night on an empty stomach.
bars:Zinfandel.why: A Tribidrag and a Plavac side by side, the family tree in two glasses.
facts: Tribidrag (Crljenak kaštelanski), then a Plavac Mali or a Babić
Evening; hours differ between listings, check before going
Walk in for the bar; +385 21 355 135 for a table (MICHELIN)

sources.label: MICHELIN Guide, Zinfandel Food & Wine Bar
